utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1778, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now can we have up on the screen, please, 65 ter 1611, please; tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this document is much, much later in time, obviously. 24th of November, 1992. And it's addressed to the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade command. And it says: "Pursuant to the directive of the Main Staff ... strictly confidential number ... and assessment of the situation, I have decided ..." How does that fit in with your observations and conclusions on the dissemination of instructions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's - I hope - quite self-evident, that the Drina Corps is passing to a subordinate brigade an instruction that it's received from the Main Staff and would seem to show a functioning chain of command. And the directive in question, I believe, has similar language in paragraph 1. And maybe more generally, although this is an area, I do hasten to add, Your Honours, that I'm not necessarily as detailed with in terms of knowledge of documents from the Krajina area; this all relates to operations in the Drina valley. And, of course, the Drina valley was one of the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serbs. To get control of the Drina valley and to eliminate the border between the FRY, or Serbia, and the SRBiH. That was a stated strategic goal. And this appears to be related to attempting to secure control of that area through the use of directives from the Main Staff down to the corps and then down onto a brigade of a lower level. And obviously in paragraph 1 it makes reference to forcing the Muslim local population to abandon areas within that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. We'll have a look at the directive in a moment. But if we continue to say with this document, as you say, it was the Drina valley. If we go over -- well, first of all, we can see it deals with Visegrad and -- under paragraph 1. And then tasks for the units, the task to the Zvornik Light Brigade in 2.1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And over the page, please, in English and also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To Bratunac. And then further down he talks about the intelligence support and engineers support. And then (c), morale and psychological preparations. "Before initiating any kind of operation, inform the unit members about the important aim of that operation and underline that the outcome of minor actions and of the whole operations of crucial importance ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please, in English. And I hope I'm on the right page in B/C/S. Yes, I am. "... importance for the realisation of the aim of the Serbian People, namely the creation and establishment of a Serbian state in these areas." And how does that fit in with the earlier documents that we saw about mobilization?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's quite similar to some of the other directives or areas, that even at the lower level the military are informing their subordinates of the importance of the territory that they are to gain control of. And, again, I say that this is an area that links to a strategic goal of a -- getting control of the Drina valley. And it would seem that they are placing an importance on informing, at the lower level, the importance of that particular area and the importance of that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It's not a rarified statement that's held at a political level that doesn't have any clear meaning. It would appear that the commander of the Drina Corps is making sure that the soldiers who are going to execute this particular operation know why it has a higher meaning or a higher strategical importance.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if we look --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honours. May that now be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1779, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we look very quickly at Directive 4 which you in fact deal with in a number of places in your report, which has got the 65 ter number 1609. It's not in -- it's going to come up on the screen, Mr. Brown. Sorry it's not in the bundle, because it was a late addition. You reference it, in fact, at your footnote number 80 in this particular section dealing with it. It sets out what has happened. If we can look at the second page in English, and it's also, I believe, the second page in B/C/S. Yeah. "Most of the tasks have been carried out in full. And among the most significant, we would stress the following. The 1st Krajina Corps has preserved and expanded the borders of the Republika Srpska; smashed enemy groups in Central Bosnia, Bosanska Posavina; liberated Bosanski Brod, Jajce, and other settlements in its area of responsibility; protected the Serbian people; and preserved the corridor through Posavina." And then if we look at the following tasks which he's decided should take place. At page 3 in English and also, I think, page 3 in the B/C/S. "I have decided the following. The main forces of VRS army of the Republika Srpska are to stabilise the Defence on the lines reached, cleanse the free territory of Republika Srpska of the remaining enemy and paramilitary formations, drive the regular Croatian army force out of our territory, while the auxiliary forces are to crush the Muslim forces in the Drina valley." So, again, that's referring back to one of the strategic goals. And then the aims of the operations are as follows.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And maybe just also on that particular page --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- not related to the Drina valley, but it makes mention that they haven't managed to achieve their goal in the Neretva river, and that was a goal. And they also ask or say that they need to expand the Posavina corridor so that even though they've secured the corridor, they want to expand on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. Can we just go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're quite right. I should have drawn your attention to that, to the previous page. Yep. The following tasks from Directive 3 have not been carried out. And there we see, as you say, the Herzegovina corps has filed to reach the left bank of the Neretva river security access to the sea. And then, finally, on this document, two other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So can we go, please, to page 4 in English. These are the aims of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Launch offensive operations to crush the HVO and the Muslims in the territory of Republika Srpska, force them into unconditionally surrendering their weapons or destroy them?"

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then over the page, again, to (d), what the Drina Corps is supposed to be doing. And I think, I'm sorry, we need to go, probably, to the next page in B/C/S. Yes, it needs to be -- sorry, yes, it's page -- in the B/C/S, it is 0087-6282 at the top. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "(d) The Drina Corps, from its present position, its main forces shall persistently defend Visegrad, the dam, Zvornik, and the corridor, while the rest of its forces, in the wider Podrinje region shall exhaust the enemy, inflict the heaviest possible losses on him, force him to leave Birac, Zepa, and Gorazde areas, together with the Muslim population." Again, how does that fit into the overall themes, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think it's as I said earlier on. This is the directive, and then that the corps - the document that we saw before - that the corps extracts its -- the Drina Corps extracts its component and passes it down to the Zvornik Brigade in relation to operations in the Drina valley, to control that territory and to move Muslims, as it's annotated on that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, thank you. That's all I ask about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1780, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Going back to your report again, Mr. Brown. From paragraph -- and we've looked at some of the examples that you specified in paragraph 1.53. You say that by -- in paragraph 1.54: "By the summer of 1992, it was clear that the objectives of creating a Serb state were not just political rhetoric but were a driving factor behind the actions of the military." And that's effectively what you've been describing to us now; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I think there are some other documents as well that are referenced. But I would argue that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. There are, in fact, a number of other references to other documents, but because of the time, I'm going to move on. Right. Yes, sorry, I'm doing -- because it's both of us speaking English, I gather what has been happening with the B/C/S witnesses, not leaving a pause. Now, the strategic goals, and finally on this part before we move to the next part of your ... were set out, were they not, very clearly in a report which deals with a number of themes. And we may as well look at that now. The analysis of the combat readiness of the army, which was produced in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's document 1305, and it's at tab 62. If we look, after the table of contents, effectively, at the beginning of that, it's page 7 in English, control and command. And in B/C/S it's on the -- it's page 8, I think. Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It talks about what's happened in the VRS and says: "The objective of our operations, battles, and engagement [sic] in the recent period has been to defend the Serbian People against genocide by the Muslim-Ustasha forces ... protect the property and cultural heritage of the Serbian People, and to liberate ... territories which are ours," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact, if we then look, please, at the third -- sorry, page 10 in English. And in B/C/S, at page 11, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it says here: "The control and command function in the framework of the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska developed in two stages. The first from April -- 1st of April to 15th of June. And the second from that date until today?" Now, the -- the establishment of the VRS took place, did it not, on the 12th of May, the 12th of May Assembly?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So when it talks about developed in two stages, what's it referring to there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I believe maybe what they're talking about is that once the army was announced at the 16th Assembly Session there was a period where, if you like, the formal structure of exactly what the corps were going to consist of, the units that were going to be subordinated, the Light Infantry Brigades that were going to be created into the TO, took a few weeks or a period to be established. And that probably meant work at the Main Staff level, maybe at the Presidency level. But once that had been agreed and accepted, there -- I think, at least according to this document, there was a formal establishment instruction which was passed out around the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That doesn't mean to say that I think when this army was established on 12th of May that they were not -- the Main Staff was somehow in a vacuum, because there are -- for example, the mobilisation instruction was passed on the 20th of May by the Presidency, passed down through the Main Staff to General Talic. He instructed that. There are reports going up from General Talic prior to the 15th of May and after the -- 15th of June and after the 12th of May, reports going up to the Main Staff, daily combat reports two or three times a day. There are instructions coming down to the Main Staff. So I think it's a little bit ambiguous, this date. But I think maybe what it meant was that around the middle of June all the pieces were in place in terms of the formal establishment structure of what each corps in the VRS was going to be. But it -- from my perspective, it didn't mean that the VRS was not functioning between it's establishment on the 12th of May and the middle of June. Far from it, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Who exactly made this analysis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This type of analysis was not unusual in the JNA. And, in fact, I suspect what happened was that the VRS, because there were many of them, were all former JNA officers, that they simply utilised this process. And it was an established process within the JNA to conduct, in essence, a retrospective analysis of how formations had been in a particular period. And I think staff officers at the Main Staff would have contributed components to this. The Main Staff officers would have been heavily involved. And I know that there were reports that went -- for example, the corps were expected to provide an analysis of combat readiness, which, in turn, would assist the staff officers at the Main Staff in compiling this analysis. So, for example, there are logistic issues, issues on tanks, communications, and I would suspect that each staff officer under whose remit that function fell would probably be the person that would provide the material for that analysis. And it would be fused together -- I don't know for a fact, but possibly by someone like the chief of operations, senior staff officer at the Main Staff, or maybe another important senior staff officer. So the information is provided by the subordinate formations, the staff officers in the particular departments within the Main Staff would most likely have provided the material that is relevant to their remits, and it would probably be pulled together by maybe the operations and training department to provide the full report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if such reports were made regularly? And were they made for purely internal purposes within the army, or were they drawn up for external purposes so as to be presented to the political leadership or others outside the military structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this is a type of document, bearing in mind its size, that was once a year or relatively -- a relatively expanded piece. But there is -- in the beginning of this document, it clearly went with a briefing. It didn't just go as an interesting thick document that went in the archive. Because at the beginning of the document it -- it's -- it gives an analysis briefing that clearly occurred. And when you look at that, it's not just military figures that are attending this briefing. It includes the political leadership. There are -- all the various departments of the army, I think, are talking about their individual component. And I believe even the minister of interior attended this briefing. So I think in this particular case -- this document was written in 1993, so it is a retrospective document. I think it's April 1993; I have to check the date, but I think it's April 1993. But it's reflecting back on what had happened in 1992, and that was the normal format of this type of report. In the JNA days it would be quite similar. But clearly this one had been accompanied - I'm assuming occurred - because there is a timetable of who is to brief --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, and if we go back -- if Your Honours -- yes, can we go back, please, to the page 4 in the English after the contents table, and we'll see that. And in B/C/S it will be at page -- it's at page 3. 5. Sorry. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I think -- the important point of my question was to shed some light over the recipients of this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who -- who were on the distribution. I'd have to check. There is a distribution at the back, potentially. But I don't know. But certainly, bearing in mind this was found in the Krajina Corps archive, it's clearly gone down the military chain. And you'd expect that. It reflects many of the issues that the army is to address. I mean, the purpose of the report is not just to look back and say, This is what happened; it's to address what they need to do in the forthcoming period. So clearly it's gone down. And clearly there's obviously a briefing that involves other people outside the military. But I can't tell you whether this document more widely was disseminated outside the military structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because the important thing is to know also whether it was pushed upwards, more particularly to the government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's signed -- yes, sorry, Your Honour, that we can do. It's signed. It's actually signed by Karadzic. If we go, please, to page 157 in English. I believe it's page 137 in the B/C/S. When I say "signed," it appears under his signature as supreme commander. It's not actually signed I don't think. It's just typed. English, please, at page 157.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have some more questions on this document, but I'm told it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So we would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have had put up on the screen the part that Mr. Brown was referring to about who was present at this briefing on the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Brown, I've had put up on the screen the part of that document that you were referring to, which is the briefing session, it would appear. And we can see that at 1330 to 1400 there were speeches by the guest participants in the analysis, the RS prime minister, RS defence minister, and the minister of the interior, who I hasten to add, in April 1993 was not, of course, Mico Stanisic. Ten minutes per speech. I would be very surprised if that was adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then over the page, please, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In fact it appears there were representatives from other armies there as well. And then finally, at 1610, contribution of the supreme commander of the armed forces of Republika Srpska to the analysis of the combat readiness. And that was, in fact, was it not, Mr. Karadzic, as we saw?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. Right. Can we then go back to the part that was dealing with. I think we've dealt with the dates that were shown about the starting. And as you deal with in your report, in fact, we can see from other documents that you reference that there were -- the Main Staff was issuing instructions and orders before its formal date of the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next -- oh, sorry. Page 11. Back to page 11 in English. And page 11 also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says how big the army was by April of 1993. "The Army of Republika Srpska currently numbers 222.727 persons..." Are you able to comment at all on that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No. I mean, I think it's at face value. That the size of the military. And the 1st Krajina Corps, I think, was around about 70.000 at that time. So it was one of the biggest, in fact, it was not -- it was the biggest by some significant way, by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we go next, please, to page 13 in English, and where they're talking about infantry units. And it's page 13 also in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you deal -- in fact, you reference this part of the report later on when you're dealing with other matters. Really the cooperation with the Territorial Defence units. But we may as well deal with this as one whole. "The infantry units which through some self-organisation grew on a massive scale out of the Territorial Defence and other units were used only at the beginning of the war according to the decisions of Crisis Staffs and similar authorative bodies. Amongst the infantry units, there were also units which represented various political structures, which were sometimes in opposition to the overall objectives of our war. Some of them developed into paramilitary formations. These units mainly executed missions in the territories of their own municipalities or even smaller areas. Initially the units elected their own commanders. And the targets of actions were chosen collectively. And individuals or groups sometimes abandoned the set goals." Now, again, really, what themes do we see, in this part, that you consider to be important?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think looking at other documentation it would seem that that first component about the use of Crisis Staffs, the referencing Territorial Defence units that ended up being incorporated into the VRS as light brigade, that would seem to be what happened. There were municipal operations in which localised TO, or former TO, light brigades were used, as well as regular VRS, I have to say. But it would seem to be -- and then what happened is these units were integrated into the VRS. And as the municipalities were brought under control, the operations tended to change, at least in the 1st Krajina Corps, into larger, more set, peace combat operations. For example, the operations in the corridor. Operations in Jajce was one, another one. So I think it would seem to be reasonably reflective of what did happen in the early -- late spring, early summer, municipality attacks with the use of Crisis Staffs at a localised level. And then what happened later in summer were the more set piece, either consolidation of the territory that they had, or larger-set peace combat operations, like occurred in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And there they refer also to the -- the units which developed into paramilitary formations. Again, is that a theme that we see echoed throughout the documentation that you've looked at, this question of these so-called paramilitary organisations?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. There were -- I -- I go back. I make no bones that there were references in the documents, the military documents, that there were what they called paramilitary groups outside the VRS that they wanted to bring in under control. I would argue that it would seem, certainly in the municipalities where the documentation is stronger, such as Prijedor, such as Sanski Most, such as Kljuc, that the units from a military perspective, although they were often operating or at least the documents say they were operating with the police and -- you know, with Crisis Staffs, the documents for me show that the units, the military units that were involved in these municipalities were not paramilitary ones. For example, the 43rd Motorised Brigade was not a paramilitary group or unit. It was a formed unit of the 5th Corps that had operated in Sanski -- in Croatia. It was sent back by Talic into Prijedor and then it [indiscernible]. The 6th brigade that we saw earlier on that was deployed back from Western Slavonia into Sanski Most was not a paramilitary group. The 1st Partisan Brigade operated in parts of Kljuc was not a paramilitary group. So, yes, there are references to paramilitaries and the problem of paramilitaries, but I wouldn't necessarily overplay them that they somehow were the units that were involved in all or many or even most, I have to say, of the actual takeover of municipalities or combat operations that were taken in controlling the territory in that first stage that they talk about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, speaking as a military expert, would you consider any military advantage for an army leadership to have such paramilitary groups operating more or less on their own? Perhaps as autonomous units that would be or could be controlled or guided on a very superior level so as to say that such groups could be asked to assist in this or that operation but other than that, these groups would be operating on their own, basically. Is there, from a military point of view, any advantage to having such groups; or are they merely a nuisance to the military leadership and the military structures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a little bit unclear. Your Honour, are you talking about from my own experience or are you talking about from what I see maybe from the documents relating to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry for being unclear. I'm talking about your evaluation of the use that these paramilitary groups in Bosnia in 1992 could have offered to the army, if any.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, depending on who they are and what their skills are and what they've done before, there could have been a value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for example, if you look at Veljko Milankovic, who clearly had some following in his municipality, who clearly had a desire to fight - I'm assuming because he sent his organisation and himself to Croatia - who continued to fight through 1992 until he was killed later in the war, of course they would have had -- and it may well have been they gained some experience or knowledge of particular areas. It may well have had some significant previous training. So from a strictly military perspective, there could have been significant value in having them within the military. But I think one of the issues potentially for Talic is that he is a former JNA man. He has been instructed that the Serbian army is to have a unified command and that -- that that should mean that anybody who is in the army or -- or an armed unit, I mean, outside maybe the Ministry of Interior, which also, you know, has an armed component, should be placed under a command. And I think I argue in the report is that, yes, he makes references to, We must disband these groups or break them up, but it strikes me that it's as much an issue of command and control as it is about the unhappiness of what these organisations -- organisations have actually done. He brings Veljko Milankovic into his corps and he gives him a task with the knowledge that this mans has created problems in the past. And I think it's almost -- but -- it is a complicated issue, I have to say, and it is -- it strikes me is that the greater goal of having a unified Serb position and a unified army counts more than the fact that these people are looting, committing crimes, are sometimes disreputable characters, and challenging what they see as the legal authority, i.e., their authority. That seems to be the problem for them. More than the really obvious one, is that, Is this the type of organisation you want to bring into a military organisation? Because I know from my own military perspective there would have been, talking about the British Army here, there is no way that I could see any commander that I have known in my military service come anywhere close to some of these groups that are outlined in some of these reports, let alone, you know, integrate them into their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Could I just put a supplementary question: Namely, if you are in possession of any evidence to show that these paramilitary groups were assigned particular tasks by the military, such as mopping-up operations or cleaning up after the takeover, do you have any evidence to support this? Or is that [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I would like to refresh my report and some of the footnotes and maybe get back to you, if I could, tomorrow on that. There are references to paramilitaries operating. I said Milinkovic was one that was integrated into the corps and send off for operations. Whether it was specifically to do cleaning up operations, I would have to look again at the documents, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you again, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, this -- the references - it may assist Mr. Brown; we may as well deal with it, if we can, now - at page 20 of the report in English, paragraph 1.26, 1.25, really, because it's Western Slavonia that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we should let the witness come back to this point, if he wishes to expand on his answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Brown, if, tomorrow morning, after you've had a chance to look through it, you come up with anything, then you can let the Court know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back, please, then, to the -- this combat readiness report. The next paragraph says: "When the army of the Republika Srpska was formed, the units were incorporated into it." If we go over the page, please, in English, and also in B/C/S, to page 14, we see there, in paragraph -- second paragraph on that page: "The [sic] infantry units formed are equipped with weapons received from the former JNA which were distributed by officers, members of the SDS, or other representatives of the Serbian People."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, again, this theme of the arming, coming from the JNA, from the SDS, and Serbs, is that a theme that had been prevalent -- sorry, prevalent, had been seen in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I said earlier I think there were some admittedly small number of reference in the documents to the arming of the Serbian TO in Western Slavonia. There were a small number of other JNA documents in the period prior to the establishment of the VRS which would indicate that the JNA were supplying weapons to TOs prior to the -- if you like, the breakup of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. It then deals with what the arms were. And then says: "Since the Muslims did not have enough weapons or support equipment, no significant support of infantry units in action was necessary, especially not by longer-range or higher range [sic] calibre ordnance. The need for it grew steadily as the war progressed." Again, from your examination and analysis of the documents, is that an accurate description, that the Muslims simply didn't have weapons or support in the way that the VRS did?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, my report didn't go into details on the issues of the Muslim capability. That's not what the report was asked to do. And it was looking specifically at the Krajina Corps documents that gave an indication. However, I would have to say that, in essence, although there was some pull-out of JNA units, to all intents and purposes, the JNA, at least in March -- February, March, April, that was present in Bosnia, became the VRS. Yes, there were individuals who left, non-Bosnian ethnicity. There was the pull-out of some equipment from the JNA. But to all intents and purposes, the JNA became the VRS. And the JNA was a military organisation that had had combat operations in Croatia over a protracted period of time. And I would, as I say, although I haven't looked at, in detail, the issue of the ABiH, I don't think -- well, I know they were not -- I believe they were not armed in anything like the way that the VRS was. I don't see the heavy artillery, I don't see tanks, I don't see communications systems, all the things that the JNA had had which used in Croatia. I don't see that with the ABiH at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And just while we're on this page - and it's purely in case anybody raises any inquiries - they describe the features of an attack at the bottom of it, and they say at number 7, or dot 7: "An attack is usually carried out by special units, so-called intervention, special or assault formations." Do you know what they mean here by "special units"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Some -- it's not completely unusual; they may call them different names, but some infantry battalions, in the way that they would have what are called rifle companies or infantry companies, occasionally have a specialist platoon or a specialist reconnaissance platoon. Often it's called "intervention platoon" in the JNA. And these may well be people who are more highly trained, highly trained in reconnaissance issues, maybe certain special weapons skills. And it may be that it's relating to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then one more question on a particular item. Two, further on, they talk about the fortification of lines during an attack is not carried out, is that ... and interdictions, very seldom. What does that mean in military parlance?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Interdiction normally means, if you like, the severance of a line of communication or an ambush on a particular route. It's to -- or to -- an attack or maybe even the mining of an area to stop the enemy utilising that route. I don't necessarily think there's anything unusual in that reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yep. Can we move on then, please, just to look at a couple of other matters in this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we go to the assessment of morale at page 45 in English, and I think it's the same in, yes, B/C/S. Or maybe it's not, actually. Just a moment. Sorry, I'm not sure it is. I think I've got the wrong ... that's a later one. Sorry, it's page 40 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "Factors which influenced the morale of units in the army" - and we'll look at some morale reports later - but "the attitude of the international community to the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis and war, and we see the Serbian People, midway through the paragraph, was subjected to inconceivable demonisation. The unscrupulous information, propaganda war, in almost all of the powerful states of the world, in particular the orchestrated planting of lies about alleged massacres of civilians, bombardment of civilian facilities, POW camps, ethnic cleansing, the raping of women, and other media fabrications serve to project a distorted picture of the national interests of the Serbian people ..." Now, Mr. Brown, from your reading of the documents, was this a position that the JNA was taking throughout, that what was being said about what was happening was propaganda and lies?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily saying the JNA, but the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the VRS. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The VRS did make such comments that, in essence, there was some external -- there was -- the external actors were misrepresenting and mis-portraying their position. And I think this -- I mean, I guess I read it like most, that what they're trying to say here is that these allegations of massacres or camps were somehow an external propaganda and that, I guess, the inferences is that they're not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then over the page, please, to the current situation in Republika Srpska, and it's in the next page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first paragraph again talks about the Serbs' problem. But it's the second paragraph I want to look at part of. In the middle of that paragraph, a series of military and political consultations that was held to consider the situation and course of combat operations, the functioning of the political authorities, and problems of cooperation between the civil authorities and the army, the numerous meetings held between unit commands, local authorities, and so on and so forth. Again, when you looked at the documents, is that paragraph reflected in those documents, namely, the meetings and the cooperation that's described here?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, I think that seems to be the case. And obviously this is a relatively general comment in one line, but do see -- if you ask me do I see examples of municipal meetings with military and civil and police, I do see that. Have I seen requests for cooperation in court? Yes, I do. Have I seen it at the senior level? Well, there are references in, for example, Mladic's diary where he is attending meetings with senior level figures but he's also touring the ground with local and municipal leaders. So if you ask me if I've seen examples that would seem to corroborate that, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move, please, to where we see the size of the Krajina Corps as a whole. Just find that. Just a moment. Thought I had it marked. Yes, if we come, please, to page -- well, let's start page 69 in English, and it's page 62 in the B/C/S. Then we see -- we've really dealt with this, the organisation of the Army of Republika Srpska and then the forming of the Main Staff. But let's go over the page then, please, two pages. Page 71 in English and 64 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And there we see, do we, that the total size of the 1st Krajina Corps on page 71 involves -- was some 72.000 men?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as you say, rightly, if we look at the size of the other corps, and this is in 1993, it really is virtually three times as large as the next largest, isn't it, which was the ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think the Drina Corps and the Sarajevo corps were quite reasonable in size, but they are still not anything like the size of the 1 KK.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just while we're on that, because we've heard a lot of references to various units or the ... can we just briefly deal with, please, what the rough size, obviously it may vary, of the various components that made up the 1st Krajina Corps or generally more than that. First of all, how many men would there be in a brigade, roughly?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, it would vary, depending on what the brigade was. If it was an armoured brigade or an artillery brigade or a light infantry brigade or an infantry brigade, so it did vary. But you could be talking thousands. Maybe 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I don't think the VRS had regiments, did it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: It did. But they were -- for example, they would have an engineering regiment, so they did use the phrase regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And what sort of the size would they [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Probably around the same size. Maybe slightly smaller than a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. A battalion?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, a battalion normally can be about 600 people. And that's kind of similar to what it would be in the British Army. But usually a battalion is maybe around 600.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: A company.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I don't know for sure for the VRS, but a company normally is about 100 to 120 men. Maybe a few more but not many more.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then a platoon?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Those ones are usually about 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, a squad?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: A squad, I know from the British Army were always impoverished, so we have fewer men than the Americans, but the -- it's usually about eight to 12 men.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if we just look at, in April 1993, we can see the total number of the VRS at page 73, in English. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just ask, before leaving the diagram on the screen. Under officers and non-commissioned officers, there are two figures above a line and under a line; what's the difference between the two? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir. Whether one relates to active military personnel and one reservists; that could be one of the issues, that the one below the line or, if you like, regular people and the others are reservists. But I'm a little bit unclear myself, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we move, please, to page 73 in English; 65 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there the total figure for the VRS in April of 1993 was 214.000 men altogether. Yep. Although you do actually reference -- well, actually, while were on the subject, just one other thing, while were on the subject of the ethnicity personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to page 80 in English, sorry, and I'm not sure which page it is, actually. It will be page -- yes. It's page 72 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where they refer to the national structure of active officers serving in the VRS: 37 Macedonians, 204 Yugoslavs, and then 33 Muslims, 62 Croats, 33 Muslims, and 200.165 Serbs. So it would appear that some Muslims and some Croats did remain with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, outside of military officers. And I think, getting back to your other point, Your Honour, I think the line does mean, I think, if you look at the figures, it says the 1 KK of the 4.054 officers established 2.373, or 59 per cent are filled with officers, of whom 398 or 17 per cent are active military officers. So I think that reflects in the figure, the lower figures, active military personnel, i.e., professional officers. Other ones are reservist, people who've had military service but have been recalled. But, yes, the figure in relation to the ethnicities relates to active personnel, but it would still seem to be relatively small.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, can we look at this report at page 90 in English, and it's page 80 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Paragraph 9: "The intensity and pace of combat operations of the army ... necessary to accommodate increasing numbers of POWs. In the past period we processed about 8.500 prisoners of war, filed criminal reports for various criminal offences against about 1.000 of them. And during the processing of prisoners of war, we pursued a policy of massive persuasion, whose effects will be apparent after a few years." In this context, did you understand what's meant by "massive persuasion"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This is under the intelligence and security section so I suspect that what they're trying to do is turn them or use them as informants. And that's what they mean. In the later years, the information they may get may be of valuable to them. Some of them, not eight and a half thousand of them, but I think, bearing in mind this is under the intelligence and security section, it may -- may mean that they're trying to persuade released POWs or POWs to somehow continue to provide information in the coming period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then under paragraph 10, in the middle of that para they're talking about cooperation, and again this is under intelligence and security. "Our cooperation with the MUP of Republika Srpska and especially with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia we consider to be unsatisfactory, that the main cause being, in our opinion, the passivity of the organ mentioned and their reluctance to expand cooperation ..." And it goes on to say at the end of the paragraph that they're going to call for meetings with the intelligence and security affairs. All right. And I think that's really all -- although, as I say, you refer to other parts. That's all that want to ask about that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1781, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, going back to your report then, Mr. Brown, you -- we stopped at paragraph 1.69, but I think I want to deal with the next part fairly quickly. Formation of the 1st Krajina Corps, effectively you cover that and give the documentation which is relevant. Then you deal, at paragraph 1.77, with mobilisation. And you set out there the background to the mobilisation order that we looked at. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look now, please, if we move through, as I say, you set this up all very clearly in your report, to the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, which is paragraph 1.83 at page 39. Now, you set out very clearly the -- where -- which area it covered. The more complicated of the municipalities was Kljuc, if we can summarize that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I think in the early part of June there was clearly some discussion between the neighbouring corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps, as to who and how Kljuc should be included and whose area of responsibility it should be in. And I think it was then subsequently passed on to the 2nd Krajina Corps, although there was a period, I think maybe late May and the first few days of June, where Kljuc, the units in Kljuc that were conducting operations in Kljuc, were part of the 1st Krajina Corps. But there was an anomaly as to exactly whose area of responsibility Kljuc fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that's pretty clearly documented and referred to in your report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can just, so that we can see a pictorial representation of it, the map. Could we have a look, please, at 10639, tab 64. Now, the copy in the bundle is pretty small, so hopefully we can blow up bits of it so it's clear what we're looking at. It has not been translated but I think you'll -- does it -- well, I suppose, actually, we ought to properly get a translation from the interpreters, if we could just -- well, if you could -- no, well, actually, it's quite complicated to get ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, what does the heading say? That's the simplest.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I believe it says "Area of Responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And if there's any doubt about it, what it says ... Then can we see, what do the markings that we can see across this?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: The one that I'm a little bit unclear on is the yellow one in the middle, the smallest one. But the -- going from top left: Ops Group Prijedor; Tactical Group 6 is the red one next to it; Tactical Group 3; Tactical Group 1; 5; 4; Ops Group Doboj; I believe this is OG Vlasic, the green one at the bottom; and then I think this is 30th Infantry Division. But the one in the middle, I'm a little bit unclear as to what that says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I hope it doesn't matter too much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we can just -- I don't know whether we can zoom in slightly --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, Mr. Brown, there's one other ... where does this map actually come from? And can you -- it's not dated, but are you able to say, from your knowledge, roughly when it was produced?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: This was a map that was within the 1st Krajina Corps collection. It's rather a large laminated map, I believe, if I remember rightly. So it was within the collection. I believe it is a map that most likely was made in late 1992. And I say that because the area of responsibility would seem to match, if you like, the furthest extent that the corps got after it secured the whole of the corridor area, which is the area to the top right, and also operations in Jajce which were in the Autumn or late summer/Autumn of 1992. So it must be at least after those operations. And my assessment is it's most likely to be in late 1992 or maybe even to early 1993. And it would seem to show where the corps had achieved its objectives or achieved its area of responsibility by that period. Although, I have to say I do caveat that with that it is not dated, and, you know, it could be a little bit later than that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And, I mean, the municipalities it covers -- actually, I think one of the documents does have a list, but it's all those going up to -- does that go up to the border with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that -- in essence, the river is the top boundary of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1782, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now in respect of Kljuc, I think you note at -- in paragraph 1.95 that military operations and attacks that had occurred there IN late May/ early June were carried out by units under Major Talic's command -- General Major Talic's command. There was then a meeting, and units were resubordinated to the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps. But I want to look at one document that you reference there, please, in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a look, please, at ... it's -- sorry. Where has it gone to? Yes. Document 65 ter 805, at tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is a document of the 31st of May, 1992. And if one goes to the third page in English and the third page, also, in B/C/S, it's signed by Colonel Galic, then-Colonel Galic. Is that the same Galic who then went on to deal with the siege of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was the 30th Infantry Division or Partisan Division, as it was called in the JNA days, in Mrkonjic Grad area, under Talic, and then a little bit later than that he went to become the corps commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And was this the 30th Partisan Division one of the divisions that came under General Talic's command?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is an order. He says: "Because of the recent situation in the municipality of Kljuc and resumption of the blood-thirsty activities of the Green Berets," and so on and so forth, "I hereby order the Kljuc Defence command shall be mounted in the zone of the municipality of Kljuc." And then he sets out who it should consist of, and it includes in that list the chief of the Kljuc public security station, the president of the municipality of Kljuc with two or three members of the current Crisis Staff, then operatives and clerks. The primary task assigned to the Kljuc defence command shall be the protection of the Serbian People in the grater area of the municipality. Now, first of all, the term "defence command," is that one that crops up regularly in documents.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No. I have to say I think this is the only time I have seen it in that phrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And do you -- from your looking at it, these documents, what was the purpose of -- of this, as far as you understand it, in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I think I put it in line with similar kind of activities that were going on in other municipalities, whereby there was a coordinated effort by municipal actors in order to conduct operations, or take control of territory, or defend territories as it sometimes may be stated, often utilizing members of the civilian authorities or involving members of the civilian authority, the police and the military. If you like, a sort of coordinated effort in that area. And there's a -- similar to occurred -- would seem to have occurred in Prijedor, for example, or in Sanski Most, where you had Crisis Staffs with a similar kind of makeup. I would put it along that. Although, I have to say, that the phrasing of "defence command" is one, as I said, that I hadn't necessarily seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In most of the documents that we've looked at so far and which we'll look at later, there's cooperation with the other authorities, the civil authorities, the police. Here it appears to be an order.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to be, which, I have to say, is the only one I have seen like that and is somewhat unusual, I suspect. But I haven't seen a similar instruction in the corps documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, could that be -- I don't think that has been admitted so far, has it? No. Your Honours, could that be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1783, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that context, I think it is also worth looking at a document, that comes from the civil side. Can we look, please, at document -- just a moment. The description of our list seems to be a bit odd. 37. Should be -- it should be a report on the work of the Crisis Staff. Can we just -- sorry. Sorry, the description is completely out of kilter of what the document is. But it's 2783, 65 ter number. All right. This is a report on the work of the Crisis Staff (War Presidency) of the Municipal Assembly Kljuc in the period from 15 May till today. And it's July of 1992. If we go to the second -- the next page in English and also in the B/C/S, we see there at the penultimate paragraph on that page in English but I think it is actually the next page in the B/C/S. Sorry, we need to go to the next page in the B/C/S. Top paragraph there? "Representatives (Commanders) of the VRS who led and conducted war operations defended the territory against Muslim extremists participated regularly at the meetings of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency at the time of the war conflict and had very good cooperation with the Crisis Staff. All important military and police issues were solved, including Crisis Staff of Municipal Assembly. The period can be characterised as a period of very successful cooperation between the Crisis Staff and military organs and the breaking the Muslim extremists's armed resistance, and the Crisis Staff especially emphasised and recognised the efforts and good job of the 30th Division," so on and so forth. And it goes on to say that: "... after the VRS regular and reserve police forces was the whole Serb population ... broke down Muslim extremists's armed resistance, and the Crisis Staff tried as much as was possible in the war conditions to establish civil authority." Taking those two documents together, Mr. Brown, what do you deduce from that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: Well, I think, at face value, the documents would appear to indicate that there was a coordinated effort to take control of that municipality involving the military, clearly, but also involving the police and the -- the civil authorities. And that there was coordination or cooperation with the Crisis Staff and the military, and it didn't seem -- at least that's what the documents would seem at face value.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it doesn't appear that in this document there is any reference at all to this -- this one document there, where it talks about "defence commands"?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: No, there's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that document then, please, be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1784, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, you then go on to deal, in your report, please, back to your report, at paragraph 1.101, "Cooperation with Civilian Bodies." And you set out there at paragraph 1.105, and it's a document we have looked at on a number of occasions - so I'm not -- although it is on our list, I'm not going to trouble the Court with that - the Djeric instructions. And you looked at the Prijedor decision of the 20th of May, which referred to those instructions. But, again -- I just want to check that one, actually. I think that's already been exhibited, so ... Oh, yes, that's the one where we've got -- there's two versions of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, one -- yes, it's the document at tab 9. I just want to check that. Yes, it is an exhibit. Your Honour, that version of the document doesn't have a date, as I say, but the gazette version, which is 466, does, which is at tab 10, and, Your Honours, I think, simply, for those purposes, we'd better ask to admit the gazette version as well, so we know exactly what the date is. But, Your Honours, I don't want to go through it again because we -- but it has already been gone through and it is an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, when you say as well --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 10, it's 65 ter 466. The previous document has already been admitted, the version of this document, but it doesn't contain a date. The gazette version does. And so I think just for those purposes, we'd better have the gazette version admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, one suggestion, Your Honours. Before we do that - make we can check - I think it's a part of the law library. But I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But I cannot be 100 percent sure, and my assistant is not in the court right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks for that reminder, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, Your Honour, I'm perfectly happy to wait until then. I withdraw that application. It's part -- Mr. Zecevic is quite right; it's part of the law library.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, as I say, I think, Mr. Brown, you deal with a number of other documents that show that in -- in your report. And, again, I don't think we need trouble that -- until we get, please, to paragraph 1.113. This may be the last matter that we deal with this afternoon. Where you reference that, in fact, it was General Mladic who ordered that contacts be established with the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and that General Talic was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. And you reference the document, which I think already has been admitted, which is the telephone numbers - yes, it has - it's P557. Can we just have that up very briefly. We see there the telephone numbers of the Krajina Autonomous Region, what is called the War Staff here. Interestingly enough, though, it has everybody's telephone number but General Talic. Are you able to read anything into that at all?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN
utterances.text: I -- I couldn't really comment why it's not there or why it should be there but isn't. I'm not sure I could really speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. In that case, I don't think I need trouble that one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see the time and that's probably a suitable time to break off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, whereas you know this quite well, I'm, nevertheless, for the record, obliged to remind you that, having been sworn in as a witness, you cannot have any communications with counsel from either side, and in such conversations that you may have outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we take the adjournment, to reconvene tomorrow at 3.15 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 12th day of January, 2011, at 3.15 p.m.
